title: The Gaussian and why it's everywhere
summary: The Gaussian (normal) distribution is a symmetric bell fixed by two numbers: the mean μ sets its centre and the standard deviation σ its width. About 68% of its probability lies within 1σ, 95% within 2σ and 99.7% within 3σ, and the central limit theorem explains why sums of many small independent effects look Gaussian.
llm_link: Neural network weights, including those of language models, are commonly initialised by sampling from a narrow Gaussian. Assuming Gaussian errors is also what makes squared error the natural loss for regression (next lesson).
key_ideas: p(x) = 1/(σ√(2π)) · exp(−(x − μ)² / (2σ²)). Changing μ slides the bell; a larger σ makes it wider and lower, keeping the area at 1.
Rule of thumb: about 68% within μ ± σ, 95% within μ ± 2σ, 99.7% within μ ± 3σ.
Central limit theorem: the sum of many independent random effects (with finite variance) tends towards a Gaussian, whatever their own shape.
One die is flat, two dice make a triangle, five dice already look like a bell.

quiz.q: You increase σ of a Gaussian from 1 to 2 and keep μ fixed. What happens to the peak height?
quiz.explain: The peak height is 1/(σ√(2π)). Doubling σ halves it, because the bell spreads out and the total area must remain 1.

quiz.q: Adult heights are roughly Gaussian with μ = 170 cm and σ = 7 cm. Predict the result: about what fraction of adults are between 156 and 184 cm?
quiz.explain: 156 and 184 are μ − 2σ and μ + 2σ, and about 95% of a Gaussian lies within two standard deviations of the mean.

quiz.q: What does the central limit theorem say?
options: Sums of many independent random effects tend towards a Gaussian, whatever shape each effect has
The mean of a Gaussian is always 0
quiz.explain: A single die is flat, not Gaussian. It is the sum of many independent effects that becomes bell-shaped.

quiz.q: The sum of two fair dice has what shape?
quiz.explain: There are six ways to make 7 but only one way to make 2 or 12, so the probabilities rise linearly to 7 and fall again.

quiz.q: A language model's weight matrices are often initialised from N(0, 0.02²). What does that mean in practice?
options: Weights start as small random numbers centred on 0, most within about ±0.04
Weights are sorted from smallest to largest
quiz.explain: Mean 0 and σ = 0.02 means small random values around 0; about 95% fall within ±2σ = ±0.04.

problems.title: The Gaussian density
problems.prompt:
Write gaussian_pdf(x, mu, sigma) that returns

p(x) = 1 / (sigma * sqrt(2*pi)) * exp(-(x - mu)**2 / (2 * sigma**2))

using math.sqrt, math.pi and math.exp. Watch the brackets: the whole sigma * sqrt(2*pi) is in the denominator.

gaussian_pdf(0, 0, 1)   # 0.3989...
gaussian_pdf(1, 0, 1)   # 0.2419...

tests.name: peak of the standard normal
tests.code:
out = gaussian_pdf(0, 0, 1)
assert abs(out - 0.3989422804) < 1e-8, f'expected 1/sqrt(2*pi) = 0.39894, got {out}'

tests.name: one sigma away
tests.code:
out = gaussian_pdf(1, 0, 1)
assert abs(out - 0.2419707245) < 1e-8, f'expected 0.24197, got {out}. Is (x - mu) squared before dividing by 2*sigma**2?'

tests.name: wider means lower
tests.code:
a, b = gaussian_pdf(0, 0, 1), gaussian_pdf(0, 0, 2)
assert abs(b - a / 2) < 1e-9, f'doubling sigma should halve the peak; got {a} and {b}. Is sigma in the denominator of the coefficient?'

tests.name: shifting mu
tests.code:
out = gaussian_pdf(5, 5, 1)
assert abs(out - 0.3989422804) < 1e-8, f'the peak moves to x = mu, so p(5) with mu = 5 should be the peak 0.39894; got {out}'

tests.name: area is about 1
tests.code:
area = sum(gaussian_pdf(-8 + 0.01 * i, 0, 1.5) * 0.01 for i in range(1600))
assert abs(area - 1) < 1e-3, f'the area under any Gaussian should be 1; a Riemann sum gave {area:.4f}'

problems.title: Sum of n dice (the central limit theorem by hand)
problems.prompt:
Write dice_sum_dist(n) that returns a list d where d[s] is the probability that n fair dice add up to s (so d has length 6*n + 1, and entries below n are 0).

Build it one die at a time: start from [1.0] (zero dice always sum to 0); adding a die spreads each existing probability p at sum s into s+1 … s+6, each getting p/6.

dice_sum_dist(1)  # [0, 1/6, 1/6, 1/6, 1/6, 1/6, 1/6]
dice_sum_dist(2)[7]  # 6/36
problems.starter:
def dice_sum_dist(n):
    d = [1.0]
    for _ in range(n):
        new = [0.0] * (len(d) + 6)
        # TODO: for each sum s with probability p in d,
        #       add p / 6 to new[s + 1] ... new[s + 6]

        d = new
    return d

tests.name: one die is flat
tests.code:
d = dice_sum_dist(1)
assert len(d) == 7, f'one die: sums 0..6, so length 7; got {len(d)}'
assert all(abs(x - 1/6) < 1e-12 for x in d[1:]), f'each face 1-6 should have 1/6, got {d}'

tests.name: two dice make a triangle
tests.code:
d = dice_sum_dist(2)
assert abs(d[7] - 6/36) < 1e-12, f'there are 6 ways to roll 7 with two dice, so 6/36; got {d[7]}'
assert abs(d[2] - 1/36) < 1e-12 and abs(d[12] - 1/36) < 1e-12, 'only one way each to roll 2 or 12'

tests.name: always a distribution
tests.code:
d = dice_sum_dist(5)
assert abs(sum(d) - 1) < 1e-9, f'probabilities must add up to 1, got {sum(d)}'

tests.name: five dice: bell around 17.5
tests.code:
d = dice_sum_dist(5)
assert abs(d[17] - d[18]) < 1e-12 and abs(d[17] - max(d)) < 1e-12, 'five dice should peak in the middle, at 17 and 18 (mean 17.5)'

hints: for s, p in enumerate(d): for f in range(1, 7): new[s + f] += p / 6
The loop over n repeats this once per die, so each die convolves the distribution once more.

problems.title: Check 68-95-99.7 with samples (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
Write fraction_within(x, k): given a NumPy array of samples x, return the fraction of samples within k standard deviations of the sample mean.

Use a boolean mask: np.abs(x - m) <= k * s gives an array of True/False, and .mean() of it is the fraction of True.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(170, 7, size=100000)
fraction_within(x, 1)   # about 0.683
fraction_within(x, 2)   # about 0.954

tests.name: one sigma
tests.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(170, 7, size=200000)
out = fraction_within(x, 1)
assert out is not None, 'returned None'
assert abs(out - 0.6827) < 0.01, f'about 68% of a Gaussian is within 1 sigma, got {out:.3f}'

tests.name: two sigma
tests.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.random.default_rng(1).normal(0, 3, size=200000)
out = fraction_within(x, 2)
assert abs(out - 0.9545) < 0.01, f'about 95% is within 2 sigma, got {out:.3f}'

tests.name: small example
tests.code:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([-1.0, 1.0, -1.0, 1.0, 10.0, -10.0])
m, s = x.mean(), x.std()
out = fraction_within(x, 1)
exp = np.mean(np.abs(x - m) <= s)
assert abs(out - exp) < 1e-12, f'expected {exp}, got {out}. Use np.abs(x - m) <= k * s'
